pos: n. (the Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1142, the first of the order in Bohemia, site of the Sedlec ossuary)
etymology: Czech Sedlec, from sedlo, a settlement or saddle of land; German Sedletz.
biblical_def: Sedlec outside Kutna Hora was founded in 1142 and settled from Waldsassen, which makes it the first Cistercian house in Bohemia and the parent of Plasy, Osek and others. It grew rich on the silver of Kutna Hora, was burned by the Hussites in 1421, and was rebuilt in the eighteenth century by Santini-Aichel in his baroque-Gothic manner. Its cemetery chapel is the Sedlec ossuary, where the bones of some forty thousand people, cleared from a burial ground that pilgrims had filled with earth from Jerusalem, were arranged in the nineteenth century into chandeliers, pyramids and a coat of arms. The dictionary records Sedlec because the ossuary preaches, whether or not it meant to. The appointment it displays is universal and single, “as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27), and Job puts the question those walls provoke without pretending to answer it himself, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14). The psalmist supplies the measure of all human duration, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15). What the bones cannot say, Paul does, and his confidence is in a place rather than in a chapel, “willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ossuary as a charnel house; a charnel-house as a place where bones are deposited; a sepulchre as a grave or tomb; mortality as the state of being subject to death; and a cemetery as a place for the burial of the dead.
webster_full: OSSUARY, n. A charnel house; a place where the bones of the dead are deposited.
CHARNEL-HOUSE, n. A place under or near churches, where the bones of the dead are reposited.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place where a dead body is interred, or deposited.
MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; also, death, actual or frequency of death.
CEMETERY, n. A place where the dead bodies of human beings are buried.
scriptures: Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
corruption_summary: Bohemia's first Cistercian house, 1142, enriched by Kutna Hora silver, whose ossuary holds the bones of some forty thousand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that mortality is a doctrine before it is a decoration. Sedlec's chandeliers of femurs were assembled as a memento mori, and the appointment they illustrate is stated once and for all, “as it is appointed unto men once to die” (Heb 9:27).

The live temptation is the one the ossuary itself risks, which is to make death a spectacle and so to blunt it. Job keeps the question open and raw, “all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come” (Job 14:14); the psalmist gives the measure without consolation, “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15); and the answer, when it comes, is not architectural but personal, “to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8).

pos: n. (the west Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1144, whose baroque convent stands on a flooded raft of oak piles)
etymology: Czech Plasy, from a local root for a flat or marshy place; German Plass.
biblical_def: Plasy in west Bohemia was founded in 1144 by Vladislaus II and settled from Langheim, the second Cistercian house in the kingdom. Its convent was rebuilt from 1711 by Jan Blazej Santini-Aichel on ground so wet that no ordinary footing would hold, and his solution was to drive thousands of oak piles into the marsh and float the building on a deliberately water-filled undercroft, since oak kept permanently wet does not rot. A system of channels keeps the water at a constant level to this day, and the whole three-storey block stands on a submerged raft. The dictionary records Plasy because it is a parable of foundations held in place by something other than itself. Scripture is emphatic that the church's footing is given and not engineered, “And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20), and the building raised on it is made of people, “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house” (1Pe 2:5). No other footing is available to be chosen, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and the builder named in the promise is Christ Himself, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pile as a large stake driven into the earth to support a building; an undercroft is a vault beneath a building; a foundation as the basis of an edifice; a corner-stone as the stone uniting two walls; and marsh as a tract of low wet land.
webster_full: PILE, n. A large stake, or a piece of timber, pointed and driven into the earth, as for the support of a building.
VAULT, n. An arched roof, so constructed that the stones sustain each other; a cellar; a cave.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground.
CORNER-STONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone.
MARSH, n. A tract of low land, usually or occasionally covered with water, or very wet and miry.
scriptures: Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: West Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1144 whose baroque convent floats on a water-filled raft of oak piles.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a foundation holds by what it rests on and not by its own mass. Santini floated three storeys on wet oak, and the apostolic account of the church's footing is likewise received rather than devised, “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20).

The live temptation is to read the engineering as the lesson and so to admire ingenuity where Scripture points at a gift. The building in view is made of persons, “an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (1Pe 2:5); the footing is not among the options, “can no man lay than that is laid” (1Co 3:11); and the builder who guarantees the work names Himself, “and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mat 16:18).

pos: n. (the north Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1196, keeping a Romanesque chapter house with a stone reading desk)
etymology: Czech osek, a place cleared by hewing, from sekat, to cut; German Ossegg.
biblical_def: Osek under the Ore Mountains was founded in 1196 by the Hrabisic family and settled from Waldsassen by way of Mashov, and its name, like Volkenroda's, records an axe. The abbey church was rebuilt in baroque, but the chapter house survives from about 1240 with its original vaulting and a rare stone lectern in the middle of the floor, carved as a twisted column, from which the rule and the martyrology were read aloud to the assembled community every day. The dictionary records Osek for that lectern, because a reading desk set in the centre of a room is an argument about authority. What a community gathers around is what governs it. Scripture is given to be read aloud and to do a particular work when it is, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16), and Timothy's charge makes public reading and exhortation the minister's business, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). The hearers are expected to check what they hear, “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), against a standard that is written and fixed, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lectern as a reading desk; a martyrology as a register of martyrs; a chapter as an assembly of a religious house; to read as to utter aloud written words; and a rule as a prescribed form of conduct.
webster_full: LECTERN, n. A reading desk, as in a church, from which the lessons are read.
MARTYROLOGY, n. A history or account of martyrs with their sufferings; a register of martyrs.
CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church; a meeting of a religious order.
READ, v.t. To utter or pronounce written or printed words, letters or characters in the proper order.
RULE, n. A prescribed form or standard of conduct or practice; government; sway.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: North Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1196 whose Romanesque chapter house keeps a stone reading desk at its centre.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what a congregation gathers around governs it. Osek set a stone lectern in the middle of its chapter house and read aloud from it daily, and the claim made for the text that belongs on such a desk is comprehensive, “and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction” (2Ti 3:16).

The live temptation at Osek was the rule and the martyrology sharing that desk with Scripture, which is how a subordinate standard quietly becomes a first one. Paul leaves no doubt what is to be preached, “Preach the word” (2Ti 4:2); the hearers are to verify rather than to defer, “These were more noble than those in Thessalonica” (Act 17:11); and the standard against which everything is tried is written, “if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (the Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1292 at Konigsaal, royal burial house of the Premyslid kings)
etymology: Czech Zbraslav, from a Slavic personal name; German Konigsaal, the king's hall.
biblical_def: Zbraslav on the Vltava above Prague was founded in 1292 by Wenceslas II on the site of a royal hunting lodge, which is why the Germans called it Konigsaal. It was intended from the first as a dynastic mausoleum, and Wenceslas II, Wenceslas III and Queen Elizabeth were buried there, the last Premyslid kings. Its abbots Otto and Peter of Zittau compiled the Chronicon Aulae Regiae, the Zbraslav Chronicle, the chief narrative source for Bohemia in that age. The Hussites burned it in 1420. The dictionary records Zbraslav as the clearest Bohemian instance of a monastery founded to serve a dynasty, and of the arrangement that lay behind such foundations: land and privilege given in exchange for perpetual masses for the founder's soul. That exchange is the thing the Reformation struck at, because it sells what Scripture gives, “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and it reintroduces exactly what the next clause excludes, “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). Grace and payment cannot be mixed, “if by grace, then is it no more of works” (Rom 11:6), and the ground of acceptance is stated negatively to shut the door, “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mausoleum as a stately monument for the dead; a chantry as a chapel endowed for the saying of mass; an obit as a funeral solemnity or office for the dead; merit as desert, claim to reward; and an endowment as a permanent provision.
webster_full: MAUSOLEUM, n. A magnificent tomb, or stately monument for the dead.
CHANTRY, n. A church or chapel endowed with lands or other revenue, for the maintenance of priests to sing mass for the souls of the donors.
OBIT, n. Funeral obsequies; also, an anniversary office for the soul of a deceased person.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles to honor or reward.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Rom 11:6
And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
corruption_summary: Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1292 built as a Premyslid mausoleum and endowed for perpetual masses, burned by the Hussites in 1420.
corruption_paragraphs: Zbraslav was endowed on a contract. Wenceslas II gave land and liberties; the monks undertook perpetual masses for the royal dead. The dictionary names that arrangement as the central ecclesiastical corruption of the age, because it puts a price on what Scripture hands over freely, “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). A gift that is purchased is not a gift, whatever the deed of foundation calls it.

Rome has not abandoned the structure. The Council of Trent affirmed the propitiatory value of masses offered for the dead, and mass stipends remain. The apostolic exclusion is placed immediately beside the gift to prevent the very mixture, “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9); Paul argues that the two principles destroy each other, “otherwise grace is no more grace” (Rom 11:6); and the cause of salvation is stated by denial before it is stated by affirmation, “by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost” (Tit 3:5).

pos: n. (the south Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1259, founded by the Rosenbergs on the Golden Trail, keeping a library of some seventy thousand volumes)
etymology: Czech vyssi brod, the upper ford; German Hohenfurth, the high ford.
biblical_def: Vyssi Brod on the upper Vltava was founded in 1259 by Vok of Rosenberg at a ford on the Golden Trail, the salt road from Austria into Bohemia, and the Rosenbergs made it their family burial house. It was never dissolved for long: suppressed by the communist government in 1950 and returned to the order in 1990, it is one of the few Cistercian houses in the Czech lands still inhabited by monks. Its library runs to some seventy thousand volumes in a painted hall, and its collection of medieval panel painting is among the finest in the country. The dictionary records Vyssi Brod for the library and for the discipline a library imposes. Books are to be weighed and not merely shelved, which is the force of the apostolic charge to cut a text straight, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), and the one book among them that claims to be more than human is identified by that claim, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19). A reader who forgets the order is warned in advance against learning that arrives as a system, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8), and the simplicity he stands to lose is named as a possession worth guarding, “your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books; a folio as a book of the largest size; philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes, also a system of principles; simplicity as plainness, freedom from artifice; and a ford as a shallow place in a river where it may be crossed.
webster_full: LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution.
FOLIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.
PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the causes of all phenomena, both of mind and of matter.
SIMPLICITY, n. Plainness; artlessness; freedom from artifice, duplicity or guile.
FORD, n. A place in a river or other water, where it may be passed by man or beast on foot.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
corruption_summary: South Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1259 on the Golden Trail, still inhabited, with a library of some seventy thousand volumes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a great library needs a ranked shelf. Vyssi Brod keeps seventy thousand volumes, and the apostolic image for handling the one that outranks the rest is a cut made straight, “a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15).

The live temptation is a learning that levels its sources, so that the prophetic word becomes one voice in a reading room. Peter ranks it above even his own eyesight, “as unto a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19); Paul names the mechanism by which a system displaces it, “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world” (Col 2:8); and he treats plainness as something a scholar can be robbed of, “as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty” (2Co 11:3).

pos: n. (the south Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1263, founded by Premysl Otakar II and named for a thorn relic)
etymology: Czech zlata koruna, the golden crown, for the relic of the crown of thorns given at its founding.
biblical_def: Zlata Koruna on the Vltava was founded in 1263 by Premysl Otakar II in thanksgiving for his victory at Kressenbrunn, and settled from Heiligenkreuz. Its name comes from its founding gift: a thorn said to be from the crown of thorns, received from Louis IX of France, in whose honour the house was styled Sancta Corona. The relic made it a pilgrimage house and a rival to the Rosenberg foundations nearby, and the abbey was repeatedly sacked in the Hussite wars. The dictionary records Zlata Koruna for the exchange its name encodes, which is a thorn traded for a crown. Scripture does allow the language of a crown, but it gives the crown to every believer without a relic, “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6), and it makes that standing the possession of a whole people rather than of a shrine, “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9). Set against that, a relic is not merely useless but a loss, and Paul reckons his own advantages in exactly those terms, “what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ” (Phi 3:7), and names what he was reaching for instead, “the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Phi 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crown as an ornament for the head denoting dignity; a thorn as a sharp woody spine; a relic as the remains of a dead body, also what is kept with veneration; a diadem as a crown, a mark of royalty; and gain as profit, advantage.
webster_full: CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by princes, as a badge of imperial or regal power.
THORN, n. A tree or shrub armed with spines; also, the spine or sharp process of a plant.
RELIC, n. The remains of a dead body; also, that which is left after the loss of the rest.
DIADEM, n. Primarily, a head-band or fillet worn by kings as a badge of royalty; a crown.
GAIN, n. Profit; advantage; interest; something obtained as an advantage.
scriptures: Rev 1:6
And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Phi 3:7
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
Phi 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
corruption_summary: South Bohemian Cistercian abbey of 1263 named for a thorn of the crown of thorns given by Louis IX.
corruption_paragraphs: Zlata Koruna was built around a thorn. The relic came from Louis IX, gave the house its name and its pilgrims, and made it worth sacking. The dictionary names the relic trade as a corruption not because splinters and thorns are absurd but because the thing they are offered to supply is already given outright: the royal standing a pilgrim travelled to touch is conferred on every believer, “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6).

The corruption survives wherever access to God is routed through an object. Peter assigns the priestly dignity to the congregation itself and not to a sanctuary, “a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9). Paul, who had religious advantages of a far better pedigree than a thorn, wrote them off, “those I counted loss for Christ” (Phi 3:7), and gave the reason in a comparison that leaves relics nowhere, “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Phi 3:8).

pos: n. (the Moravian Cistercian abbey of 1205, the first of the order in Moravia, a great pilgrimage house tied to the Cyrillo-Methodian tradition)
etymology: Czech velehrad, the great castle, from vely, great, and hrad, a fort.
biblical_def: Velehrad in Moravia was founded in 1205 by Vladislaus Henry and settled from Plasy, the first Cistercian house in the march, and its church is the largest of the order in the Czech lands. From the nineteenth century it became the chief Moravian pilgrimage goal on the strength of a tradition identifying the site with the Great Moravian capital where Cyril and Methodius preached in the ninth century, and the Velehrad congresses made it a centre of efforts toward the Eastern churches. The dictionary honours the memory of Cyril and Methodius without the tradition that has grown over it: their achievement was a Slavonic alphabet and a Slavonic liturgy, which is to say that they argued for a people hearing the Scriptures in their own speech, against those who held that only three languages were fit for it. That instinct is biblical, “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130), and it is what the written standard requires of anyone who would test a teaching, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20). The pilgrimage grown over the memory is another matter, and the warning against worship built on inherited practice is given twice over, “in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7), and “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a form of prayers for public worship; an alphabet as the letters of a language in order; a vernacular tongue as the native language; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; and tradition as the handing down of practices.
webster_full: LITURGY, n. A form of prayers; the established formulas for public worship in those churches which use them.
ALPHABET, n. The letters of a language arranged in the customary order; the series of letters which form the elements of speech.
VERNACULAR, adj. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Mar 7:7
Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Mar 7:9
And he said unto them, Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition.
corruption_summary: Moravia's first Cistercian house, 1205, grown into the chief Moravian pilgrimage goal on a Cyrillo-Methodian tradition.
corruption_paragraphs: The honourable part of Velehrad's story is the part that is oldest. Cyril and Methodius made an alphabet so that Slavs could hear the Scriptures in their own tongue, against churchmen who insisted that Hebrew, Greek and Latin alone would serve. The dictionary counts that a plain gain, on the psalmist's own ground, “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130), and on the ground that a written standard is useless to a man who cannot read it, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

The corruption is what accumulated afterwards. A site identified by tradition rather than by evidence became a devotional centre, and devotion attached itself to the place. Christ's quotation of Isaiah against exactly that process is severe, “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7), and He states the cost of the trade plainly, because a tradition kept always displaces something, “that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew pethach (H6608), an opening; Hebrew teudah (H8584), testimony; Greek mataios (G3152), vain, empty; Greek paradosis (G3862), a tradition, a thing handed over.
roots_lines: Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance; “The entrance of thy words giveth light”, Psalm 119:130.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, direction, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.
Greek maten (G3155) — in vain, to no purpose; “in vain do they worship me”, Mark 7:7.
Greek entalma (G1778) — a commandment, an injunction; “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men”, Mark 7:7.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — a tradition, a thing handed down; “that ye may keep your own tradition”, Mark 7:9.
usage: “The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — the Slavonic alphabet's real warrant.
“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7) — what grew over the memory.
“that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9) — a tradition kept always displaces something.

pos: n. (the Moravian Cistercian abbey of 1252, beside Santini's pilgrimage church of Zelena hora)
etymology: Czech zdar, a clearing made by burning, from zdariti, to burn off.
biblical_def: Zdar nad Sazavou in Moravia was founded in 1252 by Boczek of Obrany and settled from Nepomuk, and its name, like Osek's and Volkenroda's, records the clearing of ground. Its abbot Vaclav Vejmluva employed Santini-Aichel from 1710, and on the hill above the abbey Santini built the pilgrimage church of St John of Nepomuk at Zelena hora, a building laid out entirely on the number five: five entrances, five chapels, five stars, a ground plan of interlocking triangles inside a circle, because of the legend of five stars appearing over the martyr's body. The dictionary records Zdar as the most elaborate case in central Europe of a church designed as a diagram of a legend. Christ gives His people the figure of light, and gives it to them plainly and without a number scheme, “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14). The purpose assigned to that light is the Father's glory rather than a saint's, “that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16). The light Scripture calls reliable is a word and not a star, “as unto a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19), and faith that stops at a legend has no works to show, “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone” (Jam 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a star as a luminous body in the heavens; a legend as a chronicle of saints, also a fable; symmetry as due proportion of parts; a plan as a draught of a building; and allegory as a figurative discourse.
webster_full: STAR, n. An apparently luminous or lucid body in the heavens; a heavenly body.
LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints; any memorial or relation; an idle or ridiculous story.
SYMMETRY, n. A due proportion of the several parts of a body to each other; adaptation of the form of parts.
PLAN, n. A draught or form; the representation of anything drawn on a plane, as a map or chart.
ALLEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it.
scriptures: Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Jam 2:17
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
corruption_summary: Moravian Cistercian abbey of 1252 beside Santini's pilgrimage church laid out entirely on the number five.
corruption_paragraphs: Zelena hora is a legend turned into geometry. Five entrances, five chapels and five stars encode the tale of lights seen over the body of John of Nepomuk, and the whole building is an argument for a devotion. Scripture hands the figure of light to the church at large, in a sentence that needs no scheme to carry it, “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).

The corruption is the redirection, not the ingenuity. The light Christ gives is for the Father's glory and is traced to Him by those who see it, “and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16). The illumination Scripture calls dependable is a word rather than an apparition, “until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts” (2Pe 1:19), and a devotion built on a story produces nothing the apostle would count, “faith, if it hath not works, is dead” (Jam 2:17).
roots_summary: Greek phos (G5457), light; Greek lampo (G2989), to shine; Greek phosphoros (G5459), the day star; Greek nekros (G3498), dead.
roots_lines: Greek phos (G5457) — light; “Ye are the light of the world”, Matthew 5:14.
Greek lampo (G2989) — to shine, to give light; “Let your light so shine before men”, Matthew 5:16.
Greek doxazo (G1392) — to glorify, to honour; “and glorify your Father which is in heaven”, Matthew 5:16.
Greek auchmeros (G0850) — dark, murky; “a light that shineth in a dark place”, 2 Peter 1:19.
Greek nekros (G3498) — dead, lifeless; “is dead, being alone”, James 2:17.
usage: “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14) — the figure given plainly to the church.
“and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16) — whose glory the light is for.
“a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19) — a word, not an apparition.

pos: n. (the Moravian Cistercian nunnery of 1233 at Porta Coeli, keeping one of the great Romanesque-Gothic portals of central Europe)
etymology: Czech Tisnov, from tis, a yew; the abbey's own style Porta Coeli, the gate of heaven.
biblical_def: Tisnov in Moravia holds the nunnery of Porta Coeli, founded in 1233 by Queen Constance of Hungary, widow of Premysl Otakar I, who retired there and was buried in the church. Its west doorway is the thing scholars travel for: a deep recessed portal of nine orders with Christ in majesty and the apostles ranged in the jambs, carved about 1240 on the border between Romanesque and Gothic and almost undamaged. The house has been occupied by Cistercian women, with interruptions, ever since. The dictionary records Tisnov for the name over that door. Calling a convent the gate of heaven states a claim, and Scripture puts the gate elsewhere. The patriarchs looked past every built place to a city they had not built, “For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10), and the writer applies their expectation to Christians in a town, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). That city comes down rather than being raised, “I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven” (Rev 21:2), and the psalmist's estimate of the humblest place in it exceeds any abbey, “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a portal as a little gate or an arch over a door; a jamb as the side-piece of a doorway; a doorkeeper as one who guards the entrance; a gate as a large door of entrance; and a convent as a body of religious persons, also their house.
webster_full: PORTAL, n. In architecture, a little gate, where there are two gates of different dimensions; the lesser gate.
JAMB, n. A supporter; the side-piece or post of a door; the side-piece of a fireplace.
DOOR-KEEPER, n. A porter; one who guards the entrance of a house or apartment.
GATE, n. A large door which gives entrance into a walled city, a castle, a temple, or other inclosed place.
CONVENT, n. An assembly of religious persons; a body of monks or nuns; also, the house they occupy.
scriptures: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Rev 21:2
And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
corruption_summary: Moravian Cistercian nunnery of 1233 styled Porta Coeli, with a nine-order Romanesque-Gothic west portal of about 1240.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no building is the gate of heaven, however good its doorway. Tisnov carved Christ in majesty over nine orders of stonework and took the name Porta Coeli, and the patriarchs are commended for looking past exactly such places, “whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10).

The live temptation is to let a holy place substitute for the hope it was built to signify. The epistle refuses the substitution for townsmen as much as for monks, “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14); the city in view descends and is not constructed, “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev 21:2); and the psalmist measures its lowest office above any cloister, “For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand” (Psa 84:10).
roots_summary: Greek polis (G4172), a city; Greek technites (G5079), a craftsman, a builder; Greek meno (G3306), to continue; Hebrew saphaph (H5605), to stand at the threshold.
roots_lines: Greek polis (G4172) — a city; “he looked for a city which hath foundations”, Hebrews 11:10.
Greek technites (G5079) — a craftsman, an artificer; “whose builder and maker is God”, Hebrews 11:10.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain, to continue; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.
Greek katabaino (G2597) — to come down, to descend; “coming down from God out of heaven”, Revelation 21:2.
Hebrew saphaph (H5605) — to stand at the threshold, to be a doorkeeper; “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God”, Psalm 84:10.
usage: “a city which hath foundations” (Heb 11:10) — the gate is not in Moravia.
“here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) — the substitution refused.
“I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psa 84:10) — its lowest office above any cloister.

pos: n. (the Upper Lusatian Cistercian nunnery of 1234, the oldest house of the order in Germany never to have been dissolved)
etymology: German Marienthal, Mary's valley, from Tal, a valley.
biblical_def: Marienthal on the Neisse in Upper Lusatia was founded in 1234 by Kunigunde of Bohemia and has been inhabited by Cistercian women continuously since, which makes it the oldest house of the order in Germany never to have been suppressed. It came through the Hussite wars, the Reformation, the Thirty Years' War, the Prussian and Saxon partitions, the Napoleonic secularisation that swallowed Lubiaz and Krzeszow, two world wars and the German Democratic Republic. It burned to the ground in 1515 and again in 1683 and was rebuilt both times; it flooded in 2010 and was rebuilt again. The dictionary records Marienthal for sheer continuance, and for what Scripture says continuance actually is. The figure is a race, which means the virtue is not speed but patience, “let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1). Paul keeps the figure and adds the discipline it costs, “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24). The disqualifying motion is looking back, “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:62), and the psalmist's charge to a long obedience is plain and practical, “Trust in the LORD, and do good” (Psa 37:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perseverance as persistence in any business undertaken; patience as the suffering of afflictions with calmness; a race as a contest in running; to continue as to remain in a state or place; and constancy as fixedness, steadiness of mind.
webster_full: PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; continued pursuit or prosecution of any business or enterprise begun.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance.
RACE, n. A running; a rapid course or motion; a contest in running; competition.
CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in affection or purpose.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
Psa 37:3
Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.
corruption_summary: Upper Lusatian Cistercian nunnery of 1234, burned twice, flooded once, never dissolved, inhabited continuously for nearly eight centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that endurance is a virtue of pace rather than of force. Marienthal outlasted the Hussites, the Reformation, Napoleon and the German Democratic Republic, and the figure Scripture chooses for such a span puts the emphasis on patience, “the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1).

The live temptation is to read mere survival as faithfulness, which it is not; a house can persist and lose its doctrine, and several in this seam did. Paul attaches a purpose to the running, “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24); Christ names the one motion that disqualifies, “and looking back” (Luk 9:62); and the psalmist reduces a long obedience to two plain imperatives, “Trust in the LORD, and do good” (Psa 37:3).
roots_summary: Greek hupomone (G5281), patient endurance; Greek agon (G0073), a contest, a race; Greek euthetos (G2111), fit, well-placed; Hebrew batach (H0982), to trust.
roots_lines: Greek hupomone (G5281) — patient endurance, steadfastness; “let us run with patience”, Hebrews 12:1.
Greek ogkos (G3591) — a weight, a burden; “let us lay aside every weight”, Hebrews 12:1.
Greek brabeion (G1017) — a prize awarded in the games; “but one receiveth the prize?”, 1 Corinthians 9:24.
Greek euthetos (G2111) — fit, suitable, well-placed; “is fit for the kingdom of God”, Luke 9:62.
Hebrew batach (H0982) — to trust, to lean upon; “Trust in the LORD, and do good”, Psalm 37:3.
usage: “let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1) — endurance is a matter of pace.
“So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — survival is not the purpose.
“and looking back” (Luk 9:62) — the one motion that disqualifies.
